Name: attribute_lens_trajectory
Title: Reading the Answer Before It Is Spoken: Attribute Trajectories in the Residual Stream
Short Hypothesis: The object of a factual query becomes linearly decodable from the residual stream several layers before the model commits to it at the output, and the layer-wise decoding trajectory (rise time, stability) predicts whether the final answer will be correct. This gives an internal, prompt-independent readout of retrieval that ordinary logit inspection cannot provide.
Related Work: The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) and tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) decode next-token predictions layer by layer but read the output vocabulary at the final position. We instead decode the ANSWER ENTITY from the SUBJECT position using a relation-conditioned probe, tracking retrieval rather than prediction. This distinguishes retrieval dynamics from output formatting and captures answers suppressed before the final layer.
Abstract: Interpreting factual recall usually relies on the model's output distribution, but the output conflates what the model has retrieved with how it decides to say it. We propose the attribute-trajectory method: a relation-conditioned linear probe that decodes the target object from the subject token's residual stream at every layer, yielding a per-example curve of retrieval strength across depth. We hypothesize that (i) the correct object becomes decodable well before the final layer, (ii) the shape of the trajectory-its onset layer, slope, and terminal stability-carries information about answer correctness beyond the final-layer logits, and (iii) some correctly-retrieved facts show a strong mid-network trajectory that decays before output, corresponding to 'known but unsaid' failures. We evaluate on factual QA datasets across several open models, comparing trajectory features against logit-based confidence for predicting correctness and for detecting cases where the model internally represents the right answer but outputs a wrong one. We further ablate late-layer components to test whether decaying trajectories can be rescued into correct outputs. The method turns retrieval into an observable time series and offers a principled tool for diagnosing the gap between stored and expressed knowledge.
Experiments: 1. Train relation-conditioned linear probes on residual states at the subject's last token to predict the object token(s), using held-out relations for generalization checks. 2. Produce per-example layer trajectories on factual QA. 3. Extract features (onset layer, max, terminal value, area) and fit a classifier for output correctness; compare AUC to final-layer logit confidence. 4. Identify 'peak-then-decay' examples; measure how often these are output-incorrect. 5. Causal test: patch the late-layer states of decayed examples with their peak-layer states and measure recovery. Metrics: probe accuracy, correctness-prediction AUC, fraction of known-but-unsaid cases, recovery rate under patching.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probes may exploit surface correlations rather than causal features; we mitigate with causal patching. 'Decoding does not equal use' remains a caveat. Multi-token objects complicate the probe target. Generalization of probes to unseen relations may be weak, limiting the method's off-the-shelf utility.
